name: bloc
intent: Separate a feature's business logic from its presentation by routing every state change through one component: named events go in, exactly one immutable state comes out of a hot stream that the view renders.
problem: UI code and business rules are interleaved: widgets mutate shared state directly, the same state is changed from several places, a change cannot be traced back to the interaction that caused it, and testing the logic means driving the UI. The recurring trigger is that a feature's state changes should be explicit - events as the only input, states as the only output - and streamed to the view so the screen always has exactly one current state to render.
context: Reactive UI stacks (Flutter/Dart is the home ecosystem; the same shape appears in Android/Kotlin, SwiftUI, React/Angular, WPF/MAUI and Qt/QML) where a screen or feature holds state that changes asynchronously and several widgets must stay in sync. It fits when the feature's lifetime is longer than one frame, when transitions must be observable for debugging or analytics, and when business logic should be testable without a widget tree. It is a presentation-state pattern: it coordinates a feature's state, it does not replace the data layer, the router or the server's source of truth.
benefits: A single source of truth per feature: only the component emits states, so widgets cannot silently diverge and every screen always has one current state to render.

Traceability: the component records transitions as (current state, event, next state), so logs answer not only what the state is but which event caused it - the reason a plain change record is not enough for critical flows.
Testable business logic: handlers run in a plain object, so a test feeds events and asserts emitted states without a widget tree, pump loop or framework test harness.
Reusability and portability: the same component drives several screens and can outlive a UI rebuild; the view only subscribes to its state stream and dispatches events.

Discipline by construction: because the view can only send events and read states, business rules cannot quietly migrate into widgets, and new behaviour is added as a new event plus handler in one place.
Uniformity across a codebase: events, states and transitions look the same for every feature, which helps many developers work in one app and makes logging and analytics uniform.

Cross-platform code sharing: because the BLoC core is pure Dart with only stream/sink I/O, the same business logic runs in Flutter (mobile), AngularDart (web), or any other Dart target without modification.
Regulated-industry auditability: every state change is anchored to an explicit event, making BLoC suitable for compliance contexts (fintech, healthcare) where transition logs must be replayable.
tradeoffs: Boilerplate per interaction: an event type (and often a state type) must be declared for every intent, so small features pay the full ceremony of the structure.

Indirection and broken stack traces: the event is queued and dispatched through a handler registry, so a crash in a reducer no longer has the widget in its call path; you debug from the transition log instead.

Whole-state model: since only the newest state is exposed and states are immutable, every partial update must copy and update the surrounding state fields; a feature whose state is naturally fine-grained pays repeated allocation and copy cost.
One-shot effects do not fit: navigation and toasts are not states, so they end up in a separate channel or get replayed to late subscribers if they are pushed into the state stream.

Event processing policy is implicit: handlers are sequential by default, so a slow handler delays every later event, while switching to concurrent, restartable or droppable transformers changes ordering and can drop events silently.
Lifecycle discipline is mandatory: subscriptions must be cancelled and the component closed; an unclosed component keeps its state and listeners alive, and late emissions reach disposed views.
Testing discipline: if handlers capture widget or framework objects, the promised UI-free tests inherit the framework's complexity anyway.

Cubit simplicity vs Bloc traceability: Cubit's public methods bypass the event system and lose transition traceability; choosing the wrong variant for a given feature wastes either boilerplate or observability.

Equality-conflating emissions silently swallow re-emissions: if two states compare equal, Bloc skips the emission; this produces silent failures that are hard to debug when the same state is intentionally re-emitted (e.g., re-triggering a loading state).

participants.responsibility: Owns one feature's state machine: registers one handler per event type, serializes incoming events, reduces each event against the current state and emits the next state on the state stream; exposes the current state synchronously.

A simplified Bloc variant that exposes public methods instead of events; easier for features where traceability is not required but still benefits from stream-based state emission and BlocObserver integration.
An immutable value object describing something that happened (user intent, timer, repository result); the only input the component accepts and the unit of traceability.
An immutable snapshot of the feature's condition (typically a closed union of initial, loading, data and error shapes); the only output, and the thing the view renders.
The recorded relation current state -> event -> next state (transition) or current -> next state (change), published to observers for logging, debugging and analytics.
Subscribes to the state stream, renders exactly the current state, and dispatches events for user interactions; contains no business rules and never writes state.
A single hook receiving onEvent, onChange, onTransition and onError for every component, used to add logging and analytics without touching feature code.
Decides how a handler consumes its event stream - sequential, concurrent, droppable, restartable or debounced - controlling order, cancellation and backpressure per event type.
A wrapper around one or more data providers that the Bloc layer communicates with; implements the Dependency Inversion principle so the Bloc depends only on an interface and remains testable.
The lowest-level layer that performs raw I/O against databases, network APIs, or other external sources; should be generic, versatile, and contain no business logic.

use_cases: Authentication flows (unknown, authenticated, unauthenticated) where the reason for a state change matters: a logout event and a revoked-token event must be distinguishable in logs.
Multi-step forms and checkout wizards where each step is an event and the state accumulates the entered data plus validation results.
Search-as-you-type where input events must be debounced or restarted before the backend call, and results are rendered from the state stream.
Dashboard features whose state is shared by several widgets: all of them subscribe to one component, so they cannot drift out of sync.
Offline-capable mobile screens where one state union (initial, loading, data, error) drives the same UI for cache hits, network results and failures.
Feature-level analytics: because transitions are observable, user flows can be recorded as event sequences without instrumenting the widgets.
Real-time collaborative features (Firebase triggers, WebSocket streams) where a repository exposes a stream and multiple independent BLoCs react to it without knowing about each other.
Regulated-industry workflows (fintech, healthcare) where every state transition must be traceable to a specific event for compliance auditing.
Large cross-platform applications where the same business logic must run on Flutter (mobile), AngularDart (web), or other Dart targets.
Company-scale Flutter apps such as Jimdo's site-builder clients, which run BloC with a layered UI / business-logic / repository / data-provider architecture across a large team.

Android and SwiftUI codebases that adopt ports of bloc - BlocKotlin/BlocSwift (API parity with the Dart library), MewsSystems/kotlin-bloc, or arkivanov/Decompose's lifecycle-aware Component-BLoC - when they want events-in/states-out discipline outside Dart.

Open-source reference applications used as team templates - devonfw's My Thai Star and the TStore e-commerce app - which combine BLoC/Cubit with Clean Architecture, repository layers and bloc_test suites.
avoid_when: The state is local to a single widget and ephemeral (a toggle, an animation phase, a text field's focus) - the framework's own state (setState, useState, Compose mutableStateOf) is simpler and closer to the truth.
The value is a pure function of its inputs with no lifecycle, I/O or sharing - a computed value, selector or reducer function suffices.
The app is a small prototype with a few screens and no shared state - plain state holders or the framework's default state management keep the code shorter.
The data is server-owned and only fetched and cached: a repository or cache layer with streams, or a data-layer library, already gives the UI its state without an event hierarchy.
One-shot navigation or platform effects dominate the screen - those are commands and effects, not states, and a command or effect channel is the honest model.
The team has no convention for event and state naming: without that discipline the pattern degrades into ceremony with no traceability payoff.
The team is newer to reactive programming: the stream-based model, sequential event processing, and immutability expectations impose a conceptual overhead that slows delivery on small projects.

The app requires fine-grained reactivity with surgical rebuilds across a large widget tree: BLoC's whole-state model forces copy-on-write for partial updates, and without careful buildWhen/BlocSelector usage the widget tree over-rebuilds.
anti_patterns: The god component: one component for the whole application whose event list mixes unrelated features, so every change touches one giant file.
State computed in the view: widgets dispatch events but also derive or cache state locally, so the single source of truth is gone and two screens disagree.
Events that mirror widget internals ('first button pressed') instead of domain intent, which makes the transition log useless for debugging and analytics.
One-shot effects pushed through the state stream, so a navigation or snackbar state is replayed to every new subscriber or fires after the screen is gone.
Emitting from outside the component (a public mutable state field, or a handler that mutates the state object in place), which breaks immutability and traceability at once.
Never closing components and subscriptions: listeners accumulate, events are processed for disposed screens, and revisiting a feature shows state from the previous attempt.

Using Cubit public methods for features that need event traceability: if a feature's state changes must be traced back to their causing event, Cubit conceals that information and onTransition will only record Change objects without event data.

Bloc-bloc direct coupling: passing one Bloc into another's constructor creates a hard sibling dependency; when BlocA changes it may unexpectedly affect BlocB, and the dependency graph becomes unmaintainable.

Equality-conflicting emissions: emitting a state that is equal() to the current state causes Bloc to skip the emission silently, producing the notorious 'UI not updating' bug with no error or warning.

Missing buildWhen optimizations: a BlocBuilder without buildWhen rebuilds on every state change; in large widget trees this causes cascading unnecessary rebuilds unless BlocSelector or BlocSelector are used to scope what is observed.
design_principles: Single source of truth: one component owns one feature's state and is the only writer.
Unidirectional data flow: events in, states out; the view reads state and sends events, never both ways.
Separation of concerns: presentation (rendering and interaction capture) is independent of business logic (event-to-state reduction).
Immutability: a state is a new value, not a mutation, so snapshots can be compared, replayed and tested.
Open/closed: new behaviour is a new event plus handler, not changes scattered through the widget tree.
Explicit contracts: events and states are named types with a defined union, so the compiler and tests can check that every case is handled.
Dependency Inversion: BLoCs depend on repository interfaces (abstractions), not on concrete data providers; this keeps BLoCs testable and platform-agnostic.
Pure Dart core: the BLoC contains no Flutter/Dart UI imports, enabling cross-platform reuse; only the presentation layer (widgets) depends on the framework.
Lifecycle ownership: the component that creates a Bloc (via BlocProvider) is responsible for closing it; passing an externally-owned instance to BlocProvider.create causes double-close errors.
Observable transitions: every state change is recorded as a Transition (current, event, next) observable via BlocObserver.onTransition, enabling debugging, analytics and audit logs.
best_practices: Start with the reduced form (public methods that emit states directly, the Cubit shape) and graduate to full event objects only when traceability or event transformations earn the extra type.

Model states as a closed union with one shape per screen condition (initial, loading, data, error) so the view can be exhaustive and no impossible combination is representable. In Dart 3+, prefer sealed classes for compile-time exhaustiveness checking.
Keep one component per feature or screen; split rather than let an event list grow without bound.
Handle every event explicitly and keep the default sequential ordering for anything order-sensitive; apply transformers (debounce, restartable, droppable, concurrent) deliberately and document why.

Never emit a state equal to the current one (equality-conflicting streams swallow it, and re-rendering an unchanged state is waste), and never emit after close or dispose. Always check isClosed before emit inside async handlers.
Close components and cancel subscriptions at the owner's disposal; register an observer for logging and analytics in debug builds.
Keep effects at the edges: I/O belongs in handlers, but navigation, dialogs and platform channels belong in a dedicated effect channel (BlocListener) or in the view.
Test the component UI-free: build it, dispatch events, assert the emitted state sequence with bloc_test, and cover the transition log for critical flows.

Use Equatable (or sealed class equality) on all events and states; without it, Bloc compares by identity and two logically identical states are treated as different, breaking the equality-conflict skip logic.
Use buildWhen on BlocBuilder to skip unnecessary rebuilds; if the widget only depends on a subset of the state, BlocSelector scopes the rebuild to that field.
Prefer blocTest over manual stream subscription in tests; blocTest handles subscription lifecycle, teardown and async timing declaratively.
Mock at the repository boundary, not at the data provider boundary: unit tests should mock repository interfaces with mocktail and assert exact state sequences.
Never pass BuildContext into a Bloc or Cubit; extract the needed primitive values before calling add() or the Cubit method so the Bloc remains testable without a widget tree.
Never expose custom public methods on a Bloc (use add(event) only); on Cubit, public methods are the intended API but should return void or Future<void>.

Blocs must not know about other Blocs; if two features must coordinate, use a BlocListener in the presentation layer to listen to one and add events to another, or share a repository stream that both Blocs react to independently.
For regulated-industry or audit-log requirements, always use the full Bloc (not Cubit) so onTransition captures the event that caused each state change.
When using hydrated_bloc for state persistence, implement migration logic for schema changes; hydrated_bloc does not handle migrations automatically and stale serialized state can corrupt the app.
Avoid using BlocProvider.value with a manually instantiated Bloc unless you also manage the lifecycle (close) yourself; prefer BlocProvider(create: ...) for automatic lifecycle management.
Use MultiBlocProvider to flatten deeply nested BlocProvider trees, improving readability and reducing indentation.
When a state has a list or map field, always copy it on update (List.of, Map.of, or copyWith) rather than mutating the reference; mutating the same collection object breaks equality checks.
